markdown.markdown:
A simulation study was conducted in order to compare the performance of
methods for missing data handling in small-sample multilevel random
intercept models.\
The idea behind a simulation study is to carry out a computer experiment
[@morrisUsingSimulationStudies2019], where data with known
characteristics is simulated and subsequently analyzed with the methods
of interest. The analysis results can be compared to the truth, allowing
for assessment of the performance of the methods
[@siepeSimulationStudiesMethodological2024].

Planning of the simulation study followed the ADEMP structure proposed
by Siepe et al. [-@siepeSimulationStudiesMethodological2024] and will be
reported based on their guidelines.


### Data-generating model

The data-generating model is a two-level random intercept model: $$
\begin{aligned}
Y_{ij} =\gamma_{10} (X_{ij} - \bar{X.}_j) +\gamma_{01} \bar{X.}_j + \gamma_{02} W_j + u_{0j} + e_{ij} 
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-dgm}

$Y_{ij}$, $X_{ij}$ and $W_{j}$ are parameterized to have a mean of zero
and a variance of 1 on the population level.\
First, between- and within-components of $X_{ij}$ were simulated,
independent of each other and with variances chosen to achieve a
prespecified intraclass coefficient (see @sec-factors): $$ 
X_{ij} = u_{Xj} + e_{Xij},
$$ $$
u_{X_j}\sim N(0,{\tau_x}^2), \qquad e_{X_{ij}}\sim N(0,{\sigma_x}^2) 
$$ with ${\tau_x}^2 = ICC_x$ and ${\sigma_x}^2 = 1 - ICC_x$,
respectively.\
$X_{ij}$ was then group-mean-centered.\
The group-level covariate $W_{j}$ was constructed with a linear
regression equation to have a prespecified correlation with $\bar{X.}_j$
($\rho_{\bar{X}W}$):
$$ W_j=a\bar{X}_j + e_{Wj}, \qquad e_{Wj}\sim N(0,{\sigma_w}^2)  $$ The
residual variance ${\sigma_w}^2$ and the regression coefficient $a$ are
fully determined by the restriction that $Var(W_j) = 1$: $$
\begin{aligned}
{\sigma_w}^2 = 1- \rho_{\bar{X}W}^2, \\
a =\frac{\rho_{\bar{X}W}}{\sqrt{\tau_x^2+ \frac{{\sigma_x}^2 }{n} }}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the random effects on the group and the individual level were
generated as $$u_{0j}\sim N(0,\psi^2), \qquad e_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$$
and independent of each other.\
Individual and group residual variances of $Y_{ij}$ are determined by
the constraints of a prespecified residual $ICC$ of $Y_{ij}$,
$Var(Y_{ij}) = 1$ and $Var(X_{ij}) = 1$[^methods-1]:
$$ \psi^2 = ICC_{Y|X,W} \cdot (1-{{\gamma_{10}}^2(\sigma_X^2- \frac{\sigma_X^2}{n_j})+{\gamma_{01}}^2(\tau_x^2+\frac{\sigma_X^2 }{n_j}) } $$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 = (1 - ICC_{Y|X,W}) \cdot (1-{{\gamma_{10}}^2(\sigma_X^2- \frac{\sigma_X^2 }{n_j})+{\gamma_{01}}^2(\tau_x^2+\frac{\sigma_X^2 }{n_j}) }
\end{aligned}
$$ The full derivation of these equations is provided in @sec-appA.

[^methods-1]: as well as setting $\gamma_{02}$ to be zero across all
    conditions, see @sec-factors

### Missing data generation

After simulation of the complete dataset, values of the $X$-variable
have been deleted to simulate missingness. Following an approach by
Grund (2023, unpublished HTML-Document), a 'missingness tendency' $r$
was simulated for each $X$-value according to this equation: $$ 
\begin{aligned}
r_{ij}=\alpha+\beta W_j+e_{ij}, \qquad e_{ij}\sim N(0,1-\beta^2)
\end{aligned}
$$ $r_{ij}$ is a normally distributed, continuous variable. When
$r_{ij} > 0$, the $ij$-person´s $X$-values was deleted.\
The intercept $\alpha$ controls the proportion of missingness in $X$,
whereas the slope $\beta$ determines the strength of the
missing-at-random mechanism. When $\beta = 0$, missingness is completely
at random (MCAR). With increasing $\beta$, the missingness mechanism
becomes more dependent on the $W$-values; with $\beta = 1$, missingness
would be completely deterministic.

### Factors of the data-generating mechanism {#sec-factors}

A summary of simulation conditions is provided in @tbl-sim-settings. 
```{r, results='asis', echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| label: tbl-sim-settings
#| tbl-cap: "Simulation conditions for the Data-Generating Model and the Generation of Missing Values"
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
tab.cond <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c(
    "$N_1$", "$N_2$", "ICC of $X$ and $Y$", "Correlation $\\bar{X}W$",
    "Effect of $(X_{ij}-\\bar{X}_{.j})$", "Effect of $\\bar{X}_{.j}$", "Effect of $W_j$", "Pattern", "Mechanism", "Proportion"
  ),
  
  Value = c(
    "10",
    "15 / 30 / 60",
    ".1 / .3",
    ".3",
    ".2",
    "0 / .4",
    "0",
    "$X \\sim W$",
    "MCAR / MAR",
    ".3"
  )
)

kable(tab.cond, 
      format = "latex",
      escape = FALSE, 
      booktabs = TRUE,
      col.names = NULL, 
      align = c("l","l")
) %>%
  kable_styling(
    font_size = 8,
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center", 
    latex_options = c("hold_position")) %>%
  pack_rows(index = c("Data conditions" = 4, "Model parameters" = 3, "Missing values" = 3)
)
```
$N_2$ was varied ($N_2 = 15, 30, 60$), whereas $N_1$ was held constant ($N_1 = 10$). 
The effect of $\bar{X}_{.j}$ was varied ($\gamma_{01} = 0, .40$) in order to compare the methods´ behaviour with a null effect and a substantial effect. The effect of ($X_{ij}-\bar{X}_{.j}$) was held constant ($\gamma_{10} = .20$) as well as the effect of $W_{j}$ ($\gamma_{02} = 0$). With these settings, there are conditions with either a negative and a positive context effect of $X$ in the population model.
The ICC of $X$ and the residual ICC of $Y$ were varied ($\rho_X = \rho_{Y|X} = .10, .30$). Missing data were generated on X with a varying missingness mechanism (MCAR or MAR with a strength of $\beta = .30$), with a constant missingness rate of $30 \%$.
The factors were combined fully factorial, creating $3x2x2x2 = 24$ conditions.  
All in all, these settings reflect a number of the typical applications in cross-sectional and longitudinal applied research (e.g., smaller and larger intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and level-two sample sizes). They also create sufficient methodological variation to evaluate the properties of the methods of interest (e.g., null versus substantial effects).


Missing data mechanism is set to either MCAR or MAR. For MAR, the
strength of relationship between W and missing of X is set to 0.4, which
corresponds to 0.4\^2 % 100% explanation of variance in missingness
through W.
